questions.q: In orthogonal turning, if chip thickness ratio is 0.5 and rake angle is 10°, what is the shear plane angle?
questions.fact: VERDICT: The shear plane angle is 26.57°. WHY: Using Merchant's formula tan(phi) = (r * cos(alpha)) / (1 - r * sin(alpha)), where r=0.5 and alpha=10°. TRAPS: Students often forget to convert degrees to radians for trig functions or ignore the rake angle sign. HOOK: Imagine the chip sliding down a ramp; the steeper the ramp (rake), the shallower the shear plane.
questions.hint: Remember to use tangent inverse at the end.

questions.q: In a lathe operation, if the feed is 0.2 mm/rev and depth of cut is 2 mm, what is the material removal rate (MRR) formula?
questions.fact: VERDICT: MRR = V * d * f. WHY: Volume removed per minute is Cutting Speed (V) times Depth of Cut (d) times Feed (f). TRAPS: Confusing feed in mm/rev with mm/min or forgetting to multiply by speed. HOOK: Think of a rectangular prism being shaved off; volume = length (speed*time) * width (depth) * height (feed).
questions.hint: Remember V is cutting speed, not feed rate.

questions.q: Which tool material has the highest hot hardness among HSS, Carbide, Ceramics, and Cubic Boron Nitride?
questions.fact: VERDICT: CBN has the highest hot hardness. WHY: CBN retains cutting edge strength at very high temperatures (up to 1400°C), superior to Ceramics and Carbide. TRAPS: Students confuse 'toughness' (HSS) with 'hot hardness' (CBN). HOOK: Imagine a sword that doesn't soften even when the forge is hottest.

questions.q: What is the primary function of a coolant in metal cutting?
questions.fact: VERDICT: Reduces temperature and flushes chips. WHY: Coolants lower tool-workpiece interface temp to prevent diffusion wear and wash away swarf to avoid re-cutting. TRAPS: Thinking it only cools (ignores lubrication/chip flushing) or vice versa. HOOK: Imagine a car engine overheating; coolant is the radiator + oil flush combined.
questions.hint: Think of heat removal and debris clearing.

questions.q: In a milling operation, if the cutter diameter is 100 mm and feed per tooth is 0.1 mm, with 4 teeth, what is the table feed rate?
questions.fact: VERDICT: Table feed rate is 40 mm/min. WHY: Feed Rate (F) = n * z * f_z * N? No, F = (Feed per tooth) * (Number of teeth) * (Spindle Speed)? No, usually given as F = f_t * z * N is wrong. F = f_t * z * (RPM)? No. Standard: Feed Rate (mm/min) = Feed per tooth (mm/tooth) * Number of Teeth * Spindle Speed (RPM). Wait, the question didn't give RPM. It asks for table feed rate given diameter and feed per tooth? That's impossible without RPM or cutting speed. Let's adjust: 'If spindle speed is 100 RPM, cutter diameter 100mm, feed per tooth 0.1mm, 4 teeth.' Then F = 0.1 * 4 * 100 = 40 mm/min. Okay.
questions.hint: Multiply feed per tooth by teeth and RPM.

questions.q: Which process is used to join two metal pieces by melting the base metals without filler material?
questions.fact: VERDICT: Resistance Welding (specifically Spot/Seam). WHY: It uses electrical resistance heat to melt the interface, no filler rod needed. TRAPS: Confusing with Arc Welding (uses electrode/filler) or Brazing (uses filler). HOOK: Imagine two hot iron bars pressed together until they fuse.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of using a ceramic cutting tool?
questions.fact: VERDICT: High hot hardness. WHY: Ceramics maintain strength at high temperatures where carbides fail, allowing higher speeds in finishing. TRAPS: Confusing with toughness (Ceramics are brittle). HOOK: Think of a ceramic knife that stays sharp even when the food is hot.
questions.hint: They don't soften easily under heat.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a type of orthogonal cutting?
questions.fact: VERDICT: Oblique Cutting. WHY: Orthogonal cutting has the cutting edge perpendicular to the feed direction; oblique has an angle. TRAPS: Confusing with 'oblique' vs 'orthogonal' terminology. HOOK: Imagine a knife cut straight down (orthogonal) vs slicing at an angle (oblique).
questions.hint: Check the angle between tool edge and motion.
